findings.who: An accrual-method landlord whose 2025 listing campaign was invoiced in December 2025 and paid in January 2026.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks for advertising 'paid in 2025'. Nothing was paid in 2025, so the filer truthfully answers no or enters zero, even though the expense was incurred in 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses' (no 'paid' limit in the general instructions for lines 5 through 21)
findings.fix: Ask for advertising 'paid (or, if you use the accrual method, incurred) in 2025', or ask the accounting method first and word the question to match.

findings.who: An owner of a royalty property, such as a copyright, patent or NIL licensing deal reported on Schedule E, who paid to market the work to licensees in 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate and question say 'For this rental property' and 'Advertising for renters'. A royalty owner has no renters and no rental property, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column.'
findings.fix: Say 'For this rental or royalty property — advertising or marketing to find tenants, licensees or other payers'.

findings.who: A landlord who paid listing fees on Zillow or Apartments.com, a promoted Craigslist post, or yard signs, and does not think of these as 'advertising'.
findings.why_no: The bare gate word 'Advertising' suggests newspaper, radio or online display ads. Listing fees and signs do not feel like advertising, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses'
findings.fix: Add examples to the help text: 'listing-site fees, promoted posts, signs, flyers and other costs to find tenants'.

findings.who: A landlord whose property manager placed and paid for vacancy ads and deducted the cost from the rent sent to the owner. The owner only sees a net remittance on a statement.
findings.why_no: The question says 'paid in 2025'. The owner never wrote a check for advertising, so they believe they did not pay it.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... management fees, agents’ commissions'
findings.fix: Add: 'Include advertising your property manager or agent paid on your behalf, such as amounts deducted from rent they sent you (see your owner statement).'

findings.who: Any filer who reads the gate as shown.
findings.why_no: The gate text is only 'For this rental property — Advertising', with no verb or time frame. The filer cannot tell what a yes means: whether they advertised, whether they paid, or in what year.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21
findings.fix: Reword the gate: 'For this rental or royalty property, did you have any advertising or marketing costs for 2025 (paid by you or by an agent for you)?'

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A short-term rental host whose platform or property manager pays the cleaners and takes the fees out of each payout. The host never writes a check to a cleaner and sees only net deposits.
findings.why_no: The gate is just the label 'Cleaning and maintenance' with no help text. A host who thinks only of payments they made themselves answers no, because the cleaning was netted out by someone else.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property ... You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you, or a platform or manager acting for you, pay for cleaning, cleaning supplies, or routine upkeep of this property? Include cleaning fees taken out of platform payouts or manager statements.' Tell the filer to report gross rents, not net payouts.

findings.who: A landlord who paid for routine upkeep that is not cleaning: a gardener or lawn service, snow removal, pest control, pool service, HVAC filter or gutter service. They paid no cleaning crew.
findings.why_no: They read 'Cleaning and maintenance' as cleaning only. Or they think of 'maintenance' as repairs, which the follow-up question excludes ('not repairs'), and decide no amount of theirs belongs here.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees...'
findings.fix: In the gate help, list examples: janitorial and turnover cleaning, landscaping, snow removal, pest control, pool service, and routine servicing. Explain that fixing something broken is a repair and goes on line 14.

findings.who: A landlord who uses the accrual method. Cleaning or maintenance was done and billed in December 2025, but the bill was paid in January 2026.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks for amounts 'paid in 2025', and the help says 'paid in 2025'. An accrual-method filer incurred the expense in 2025 but paid nothing that year, so they answer no or enter zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property'; the same page uses 'paid or incurred in 2025' for related expenses
findings.fix: Ask for cleaning and maintenance 'paid in 2025 (or incurred in 2025 if you use the accrual method)'.

findings.who: Any filer who sees a gate that is only a bare label, 'For this rental property — Cleaning and maintenance', without a question or a year.
findings.why_no: No year, no verb and no examples are given. The filer must guess whether the gate asks if the property was cleaned, if they cleaned it themselves (own labor, not deductible), or if they paid someone. Someone who did some of the work themselves and paid for the rest may answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Do not deduct the value of your own labor'
findings.fix: Phrase the gate as a question: 'Did you pay (or owe) any amount in 2025 for cleaning or routine maintenance of this property, including supplies, but not counting your own labor?'

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse owns or manages the rental property and paid the leasing commission from the spouse's funds; the filer personally paid none.
findings.why_no: The gate says only 'For this rental property — Commissions' and does not say 'you or your spouse'; the filer reads it as asking about the filer's own commissions and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... agents’ commissions ...'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse have any commissions for this rental property?' and make clear that either spouse's payment is included.

findings.who: A filer who rents a room or part of their home and paid an agent a commission to find a tenant for the house, with no commission separately allocated to the rented room.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'this rental property' as a separate rental property, not a partly rented home, and answers no because the commission was for the whole house.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Renting out part of your home. If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part.'
findings.fix: Gate should include 'a room or part of your home' and state that the full commission is entered before dividing out personal use.

findings.who: A filer who paid a flat 'leasing fee,' 'finder's fee,' or 'renewal fee' to the person who found or kept a tenant, including a fee withheld from rent, rather than an amount labeled 'commission.'
findings.why_no: The gate uses only the word 'Commissions'; the filer answers no because the charge was called a fee and was not paid separately as a commission.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... agents’ commissions ...'
findings.fix: Ask about 'commissions or fees paid to an agent, property manager, or platform for finding, renewing, or keeping a tenant, including amounts withheld from rent.'

findings.who: A filer who owned and rented the property earlier in 2025, paid a leasing commission, and then sold or converted the property before year-end.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'For this rental property' as requiring that the property still be a rental property at the time of filing and answers no because they no longer own or rent it.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column. You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... agents’ commissions ...'
findings.fix: Ask about property rented at any time during 2025, including before a sale or conversion.

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A married filer filing jointly whose spouse alone owns and rents the property and holds the insurance policy; the filer personally has no rental property and no policy in their own name.
findings.why_no: The gate says only 'For this rental property — Insurance' and does not say 'you or your spouse,' so the filer answers no for themselves even though the spouse's premium belongs on the joint return.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column. You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance...'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse have insurance for this rental property?' and treat the spouse's policy as yes on a joint return.

findings.who: A filer paid a two- or three-year rental insurance premium in 2024 or earlier covering 2025, so the property has 2025 coverage but no insurance payment was made in 2025.
findings.why_no: They read the one-word gate 'Insurance' as asking about insurance paid or billed this year and answer no because they wrote no 2025 premium check; the multi-year proration instruction appears only after yes.
findings.irs_text: p527 p. 5: 'If you pay an insurance premium for more than 1 year in advance, you can’t deduct the total premium in the year you pay it. For each year of coverage, you can deduct only the part of the premium payment that applies to that year.'
findings.fix: Gate on 'Did you have insurance covering this rental property at any time in 2025, even if paid in an earlier year?' or show the prepaid/multi-year help before the gate.

findings.who: A filer rents a room or part of their home and has a homeowners insurance policy, but no separate landlord or rental-specific policy.
findings.why_no: They read 'For this rental property — Insurance' as asking for a rental-property policy and answer no because they only have homeowners insurance; the allocable part of that premium is still a rental expense.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Renting out part of your home. If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part.' The same page lists insurance as a deductible rental expense.
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to ask about any homeowners or rental insurance covering the property, including a policy not labeled as rental insurance.

findings.who: A filer's rental property insurance premium is paid by the mortgage servicer from an escrow account, so the filer never writes a separate check to the insurance company.
findings.why_no: They answer no to 'For this rental property — Insurance' because they did not pay an insurance bill directly; the escrow disbursement is still their insurance expense.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents’ commissions, and depreciation.'
findings.fix: Ask whether insurance was paid from any source, including mortgage escrow, a property manager, or a closing statement, and include those examples before the gate.

findings.who: A filer owns a rented condominium where the HOA master policy covers the building and the filer pays only a rental liability or umbrella policy; there is no separate property policy 'on' the building.
findings.why_no: They answer no because they read 'Insurance' or 'Insurance on it' as property insurance only, not liability or umbrella coverage for the rental activity.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents’ commissions, and depreciation.'
findings.fix: Clarify that insurance includes liability, umbrella, and other rental-related coverage, not just a policy insuring the building.

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21
p. 5, Insurance premiums paid in advance, "For each year of coverage, you can deduct only the part of the premium payment that applies to that year"

findings.who: A filer who has a royalty property (including one who also has a rental property) and paid an accountant or tax preparer for tax advice or preparation of forms for the royalty property, but paid no legal or professional fees for the rental property.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only 'For this rental property — Legal and other professional fees.' They truthfully answer no for the rental property, and the royalty property's line-10 fees are never reached.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 10: 'Include on line 10 fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms related to your rental real estate or royalty properties.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to 'For this rental or royalty property' or use a Schedule E line-10 gate that covers both rental real estate and royalty properties.

findings.who: A filer with a rental property who paid a tax preparer or accountant for tax advice or for preparing the rental portion of the return, but paid no attorney or conventional legal fee.
findings.why_no: They read 'Legal and other professional fees' as a legal-fee question and answer no because no lawyer was involved; the tax-preparation example appears only in the gated question after the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 10: 'Include on line 10 fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms related to your rental real estate or royalty properties.'
findings.fix: Put the examples in the gate: 'Did you pay any legal, tax-preparation, accounting, or other professional fees for this rental?'

findings.who: A married filer filing jointly whose spouse paid the rental property's tax-preparation, accounting, or legal fees, while the filer personally paid none.
findings.why_no: The gate says only 'For this rental property — Legal and other professional fees' and does not say 'you or your spouse'; the filer reads it as asking about their own fees and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 10: 'Include on line 10 fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms related to your rental real estate or royalty properties.'
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse pay...' or make the gate explicitly property-level on the joint return.

findings.who: A filer who rented out a property for part of 2025 and sold it during 2025, and who paid deductible legal or professional fees for the rental before the sale, such as lease-review legal fees or tax advice for the rental.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'For this rental property' in the present tense; after the sale they no longer have a rental property and answer no, even though the 2025 Schedule E line 10 takes the pre-sale fees.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 10: 'Include on line 10 fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms related to your rental real estate...' and the general lines 5-21 instruction to 'deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses' for the rental.
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you rent out or own this property at any time in 2025, including a property sold during the year?'

findings.who: A filer who paid one tax-preparation or accounting fee covering both personal and rental matters, with no separate rental invoice.
findings.why_no: They read the gate as asking for fees paid specifically and separately for the rental property, so they answer no; but the rental-related portion of the combined fee is line 10.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, Line 10: 'Include on line 10 fees for tax advice and the preparation of tax forms related to your rental real estate or royalty properties.'
findings.fix: Ask whether any part of a legal, professional, tax-preparation, or accounting fee related to the rental, even if billed together with personal matters, and allow allocation.

locators: p. 6, Line 10

findings.who: A filer sold or otherwise disposed of a rental property in 2025, financed partly with a seller-carryback nonrecourse note. Rents exceeded expenses, so Schedule E line 21 is zero or positive, but the disposition produced a loss on Form 4797.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from line 21 alone, so the filer is never asked. The at-risk loss for the activity includes the loss on disposing of its assets, which is reported outside line 21.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3, At-Risk Rules: "The at-risk rules in most cases limit the amount of loss (including loss on the disposition of assets) you can claim to the amount you could actually lose in the activity."
findings.fix: Ask the not-at-risk question when the activity has an overall loss, counting line 21 and any loss on disposing of the activity's property (Form 4797 or Form 8949). Better, ask it whenever the property has any not-at-risk financing, and decide whether Form 6198 is needed after a yes.

findings.who: A filer had a 2024 rental loss that the at-risk rules disallowed, so it carries to 2025. The filer enters only 2025 income and expenses, which net to a gain, so line 21 shows no loss.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from this year's figures. The prior-year disallowed amount is a deduction from the same activity this year, so Form 6198 may still be needed. The filer never sees a question about it.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 21: "If you have amounts for which you are not at risk, use Form 6198 to determine the amount of your deductible loss"; p. 3: "In most cases, you must complete Form 6198 to figure your loss if you have ... Amounts in the activity for which you are not at risk."
findings.fix: Before computing the gate, ask: "Did you or your spouse have a loss from this property in an earlier year that you could not deduct because of the at-risk rules (Form 6198)?" A yes forces the question, or a refusal.

findings.who: A filer reports a royalty or other mineral property interest in Part I, bought with a nonrecourse loan from a bank. Line 21 is a loss.
findings.why_no: The help says "A mortgage from a bank, a government or another regular lender is at risk," and the question covers only borrowing "from anyone but a bank or regular lender." Qualified nonrecourse financing does not cover mineral property, so this bank loan is not at risk.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "Qualified nonrecourse financing is financing for which no one is personally liable for repayment and is: • Borrowed by you in connection with the activity of holding real property (other than mineral property)"
findings.fix: Limit the bank exception to real property other than mineral property. Add to the help: "For oil, gas, mineral or royalty interests, a loan with no personal liability is a Yes even from a bank."

findings.who: Joint filers whose spouse put in the not-at-risk money for a jointly reported property, for example through a nonrecourse loan from the spouse's relative who co-owns the property.
findings.why_no: The question asks "Was any money you put in ...". The filer answering reads "you" as themselves.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "Amounts borrowed for use in the activity from a person who has an interest in the activity (other than as a creditor) or who is related under section 465(b)(3)(C) to a person (other than you) having such an interest."
findings.fix: Say "you or your spouse" throughout the question and help.

findings.who: A filer whose investment in the property is protected by a stop-loss or guarantee arrangement, but who contributed property rather than cash, or used a loan to buy the property rather than to "put money in."
findings.why_no: "Money you put in" reads as the filer's own cash contribution. It misses contributed property, borrowed amounts used to acquire the property, and amounts used to acquire an interest in the activity.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "Cash, property, or borrowed amounts used in the activity (or contributed to the activity, or used to acquire your interest in the activity) that are protected against loss by a guarantee, stop-loss agreement, or other similar arrangement"
findings.fix: Reword: "Was any cash, property, or loan used to buy, improve, or operate this property, or to buy your share of it, ..." Name the acquisition loan explicitly.

findings.who: A filer with a nonrecourse loan from a regular lender that is related to the filer on non-commercial terms, or that receives a fee because of the filer's investment (for example, a promoter-affiliated lender).
findings.why_no: The help reads as a complete rule: a regular lender is at risk, and only the seller, a co-owner, or their relatives make it a Yes. A lender related to the filer, or a fee-earning lender, is not mentioned.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 3: "A qualified person cannot be: • Related to you (unless the nonrecourse financing obtained is commercially reasonable ...), • The seller of the property (or a person related to the seller), or • A person who receives a fee due to your investment in real property (or a person related to that person)."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "A lender related to you on non-market terms, or one that gets a fee because of your investment, is also a Yes if you are not personally liable."

locators: p. 3, At-Risk Rules, "In most cases, you are not at risk for amounts such as the following", and Qualified nonrecourse financing
p. 7, Line 21
p. 7, Line 21, "If you have amounts for which you are not at risk, use Form 6198 to determine the amount of your deductible loss"

findings.who: A landlord whose property management company collects the rent, keeps its percentage fee, and sends the owner only the net amount. The owner never writes a check to the manager.
findings.why_no: The gate's bare words 'Management fees', and the gated input's 'paid in 2025', suggest a bill the owner paid. A fee kept out of rent that the owner never handled does not feel paid, so the owner ticks no. The owner may also report the net deposit as rent.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents' commissions, and depreciation.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you or anyone acting for you (a property manager, rental agent, or co-host) charge a management fee for this property, including fees taken out of rent before it reached you?' Help text: report gross rent on line 3 and the withheld fee here.

findings.who: A short-term or vacation rental host who pays a co-host or vacation-rental management company a percentage of bookings for listing, guest handling, and turnover coordination.
findings.why_no: The host reads 'Management fees' as a traditional long-term property management contract. A co-host share or a 'service fee' does not look like one, so the host answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... management fees, agents' commissions ...'
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Includes fees to property managers, co-hosts, and vacation-rental management companies for running the rental, whether a flat fee or a percentage of rent.'

findings.who: An owner of a royalty property, such as a mineral or oil and gas interest, who pays a mineral management firm a fee to administer leases and collect royalties. The property is entered in a Schedule E column.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'For this rental property'. A royalty owner truthfully holds no rental property, so they answer no or skip the question, although Schedule E line 11 applies to every column.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21: 'Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column. You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... management fees ...'
findings.fix: Word the gate per property: 'For this rental or royalty property, did you pay or incur management fees?'

findings.who: A rare individual landlord on the accrual method who incurred December 2025 management fees but paid them in January 2026.
findings.why_no: The gated input asks for fees 'paid in 2025', so the filer may answer no or enter zero. Under the accrual method the expense belongs to 2025.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as ... management fees ...' (the instructions elsewhere use 'paid or incurred in 2025')
findings.fix: Change the wording to 'paid (or, if you use the accrual method, incurred) for 2025'.

findings.who: Any filer who reaches the gate.
findings.why_no: The gate text 'For this rental property — Management fees' is a label, not a question. A filer may not know whether to tick it or what ticking means.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21
findings.fix: Word it as a question: 'For this property, did you or your spouse pay, or have deducted from rents, any management fees in 2025?'

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A filer uses an unsecured loan, credit card, or line of credit to buy, improve, or maintain a rental property and has no mortgage on the rental itself.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about a mortgage/has_mortgage, so they truthfully answer no; they do not think ordinary loan or credit-card interest is 'mortgage interest.'
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'In most cases, to determine the interest expense allocable to your rental activities, you must have records to show how the proceeds of each debt were used.'
findings.fix: Ask broadly whether the filer paid interest on any debt whose proceeds were used for this rental, including unsecured debt and credit cards, then ask for the allocable amount.

findings.who: A filer takes a home equity loan or other loan secured by their personal residence and uses the proceeds for the rental property, so the rental itself has no mortgage.
findings.why_no: They read 'For this rental property—mortgage interest' as requiring a mortgage secured by the rental, and answer no because the mortgage is on their home.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'In general, you allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds. You allocate loan proceeds by tracing disbursements to specific uses.'
findings.fix: Gate on interest on any debt traced to the rental, not on whether the rental property itself is collateral; mention home equity and other debt in the gate.

findings.who: A filer rents out part of their home or an ADU and pays mortgage interest on the home; there is no separate mortgage labeled as belonging to the rental portion.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'For this rental property—mortgage interest,' which they read as asking for a separate rental-property mortgage, not the home mortgage that partly finances the rented space.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Renting out part of your home. If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part.'
findings.fix: Ask whether the property was rented or offered for rent for any part of 2025 and whether there was mortgage interest on it; allocate after a broad yes.

findings.who: A filer pays mortgage interest to a seller, private individual, or foreign lender on a rental property and receives no Form 1098.
findings.why_no: The gate names 'banks, etc.' and the gated amount is tied to Form 1098, so they answer no because no bank or Form 1098 is involved.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'In most cases, to determine the interest expense allocable to your rental activities, you must have records to show how the proceeds of each debt were used.'
findings.fix: Ask whether interest was paid on a rental-property debt to any lender, not only banks or Form 1098 issuers.

findings.who: A married filer files jointly, but only the spouse owns the rental property and pays its mortgage; the filer personally has no mortgage.
findings.why_no: The gate uses 'the filer'/'you' without saying 'you or your spouse,' so they answer no for themselves even though the joint return includes the spouse's rental.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: 'Enter your total expenses for mortgage interest (line 12) ... even if you have only one property.'
findings.fix: For a joint return, state 'you or your spouse' and ask about any rental property included on the joint return.

locators: p. 6, Lines 12 and 13

findings.who: A filer who deducts actual auto expenses for the rental activity and has auto rental or lease payments for a leased vehicle or a rented car used in that activity, including a multiyear vehicle lease.
findings.why_no: The gate just says 'Other.' The filer truthfully reads that as miscellaneous costs and says no because the payment is an auto/lease expense, not 'other'; the gated help also says not to use line 19 for anything that lasts more than a year, which a multiyear vehicle lease appears to do.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6: 'Show auto rental or lease payments on line 19 and depreciation on line 18.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to ask 'Any other Schedule E line 19 expenses, including auto rental or lease payments?' and state that vehicle rental/lease payments go on line 19 even when the lease term exceeds one year.

findings.who: A filer who elects the deduction for qualified costs to remove architectural or transportation barriers for individuals with disabilities or the elderly and has no other line 19 expense.
findings.why_no: The gate says only 'Other'; the filer treats the barrier-removal cost as an improvement/capital item and, per the help, lists it with the buildings instead of answering yes to an other rental expense.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6: 'You can also elect to deduct up to $15,000 of qualified costs paid or incurred in 2025 to remove architectural or transportation barriers to individuals with disabilities and the elderly.'
findings.fix: Mention the barrier-removal election in the gate/help as a line 19 other expense and carve it out of the 'improvement' exclusion.

locators: p. 6, Line 19

findings.who: A filer paid points or loan fees in 2025 to obtain or refinance a loan used for the rental property, but paid no amount separately labeled 'interest'.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about 'Other interest'; points and loan fees are not 'interest' in ordinary reading, so the filer ticks no. The gated line would include 2025's amortized share of those points or loan fees.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: '...determine the interest expense allocable to your rental activities...'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to 'Other interest, points, or loan fees on loans used for this rental property (including only 2025's amortized share).'

findings.who: A filer paid mortgage interest to the seller or another private lender under seller financing for the rental property; no Form 1098 was issued in the filer's name.
findings.why_no: They read 'Other interest' as interest other than mortgage interest. Because their interest is mortgage interest, they answer no, though line 13 is for interest on rental-property loans not reported on Form 1098 in their name.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: '...allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds...'
findings.fix: Gate on the fact: 'Did you pay interest on any loan used for this rental property that is not reported on a Form 1098 in your name?'

findings.who: A filer took a home equity or other loan secured by their personal residence and used the proceeds to buy, improve, or maintain the rental property; the loan is not secured by the rental property.
findings.why_no: They read 'For this rental property — Other interest' as requiring the loan to be secured by or made for the rental property itself, so they answer no. The instructions allocate interest by tracing the loan proceeds to their specific uses.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: 'You allocate loan proceeds by tracing disbursements to specific uses.'
findings.fix: State in the gate that interest on any debt whose proceeds were used for the rental property counts, even if the loan is secured by another property.

findings.who: A filer used only part of a loan for the rental property and part for personal expenses, or rented only part of a home, so only the rental-allocable share of interest is deductible.
findings.why_no: They read the gate as requiring the entire interest to be for the rental property; because part was personal, they answer no. The instructions require allocating interest to the rental activities and the help says to enter only the rental part.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: '...determine the interest expense allocable to your rental activities...'
findings.fix: State in the gate that interest allocated to the rental property counts even if the loan or property was also used personally.

findings.who: A married filing jointly filer whose spouse alone paid other interest on a rental-property loan, such as a private loan, and the filer personally paid none.
findings.why_no: The gate does not say 'you or your spouse,' and the gated question says 'no Form 1098 in your name'; the filer reads it as their own interest and answers no, omitting the spouse's line 13 amount from the joint return.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: '...interest expense allocable to your rental activities...'
findings.fix: Use 'you or your spouse' and ask about 'any loan used for this rental property, whether in your name, your spouse's name, or both.'

findings.who: A filer paid points or loan fees in an earlier year to obtain the rental-property loan and has a 2025 amortization share, but paid no new interest or points in 2025.
findings.why_no: They read 'Other interest' as a current payment and know they paid nothing this year; the gated question would include only 2025's spread share of the earlier points or loan fees.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: '...allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds...'
findings.fix: Ask in the gate about '2025's share of points or loan fees from any year,' not only interest paid in 2025.

findings.who: A filer co-owns the rental property with a non-spouse and pays their share of mortgage interest, but the lender issued Form 1098 only to the co-owner; no Form 1098 is in the filer's name.
findings.why_no: They see a Form 1098 for the mortgage and read 'Other interest' as not applying to mortgage interest. Line 13 covers their share when no Form 1098 is in their name.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 6, Lines 12 and 13: '...allocate interest on a loan the same way you allocate the loan proceeds...'
findings.fix: Gate on 'interest on a loan used for this rental property not reported on a Form 1098 in your name,' and mention co-owner statements.

locators: p. 6, Lines 12 and 13

findings.who: A landlord who paid only for routine upkeep in 2025, such as repainting a unit between tenants, servicing the furnace, cleaning gutters, or pest treatment. Nothing broke and nothing was fixed.
findings.why_no: The gate says only "Repairs". The filer reads that as fixing something broken and answers no, because the work was maintenance, not a repair.
findings.irs_text: "You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance... Examples are fixing a broken lock or painting a room." (i1040se 2025 p. 7, Line 14)
findings.fix: Ask: "For this rental property, did you or your spouse pay for any repairs or maintenance that keep it in working order (for example fixing a lock, painting a room, servicing equipment, cleaning or pest control)? Do not count improvements."

findings.who: A landlord who patched part of a roof, replaced a few shingles, or fixed one furnace component in 2025.
findings.why_no: The help says "A new roof, a new furnace or an addition is an improvement, not a repair". The filer sees roof or furnace work named as an improvement and answers no, even though a partial fix that only keeps the system working is a repair.
findings.irs_text: "Repairs and maintenance costs are those costs that keep the property in an ordinarily efficient operating condition... improvements are amounts paid to better or restore your property... Examples of improvements are... replacing an entire HVAC system." (i1040se 2025 p. 7, Line 14)
findings.fix: Reword the help: "Replacing an entire roof, HVAC system or furnace, or adding to the building, is an improvement. Fixing or patching part of one (a leak, a few shingles, a failed part) is a repair."

findings.who: A landlord whose tenant paid for a repair and deducted it from rent, or whose property manager paid repairs out of collected rents and sent only the net amount.
findings.why_no: The filer did not write the check, so they believe they had no repairs to report. They also report only the net rent they received.
findings.irs_text: "You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance." (i1040se 2025 p. 7, Line 14)
findings.fix: Add to the gate: "Include repairs a tenant or property manager paid on your behalf, for example deducted from rent or paid out of rents collected; report the gross rent on line 3."

findings.who: A landlord whose repair was done in December 2024 but whose invoice was paid in January 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate does not say which year counts. The filer associates the repair with 2024 and answers no for the 2025 return.
findings.irs_text: "You can deduct the amounts paid for repairs and maintenance." (i1040se 2025 p. 7, Line 14)
findings.fix: State the timing in the gate: "Did you pay anything in 2025 for repairs or maintenance, including work done in an earlier year but paid in 2025?"

locators: p. 7, Line 14

findings.who: A filer who rents out only part of their home (or a vacation property for part of the year) and buys ordinary household supplies, such as cleaning products and paper goods, used in both the rented and personal portions.
findings.why_no: They answer no because the supplies were not bought solely or specifically for the rental property; the gate does not say to include a shared supply before dividing out personal use.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part.
findings.fix: Ask whether any supplies were used in or for the rental property, including shared household or vacation-property supplies; compute the rental-use percentage after a broad yes, as the helper says before any division for personal use.

findings.who: A filer who owns several rental properties and buys cleaning or repair supplies in bulk for all of them, then answers the per-property question no for one property because no supplies were separately purchased for that property.
findings.why_no: The gate says For this rental property — Supplies; the filer reads that as requiring supplies dedicated to that property, not a bulk purchase that must be allocated among properties.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column.
findings.fix: Gate on supplies used in any rental property or bought in bulk for rental use, then allocate the portion to this property; do not require separate purchase for each property.

findings.who: On a joint return, the filer's spouse solely owns the rental property and paid for its supplies; the filer answers no because the supplies were the spouse's, not the filer's.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only For this rental property — Supplies and does not say you or your spouse; the filer reads it as asking about the filer's own supplies.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: Enter your rental and royalty expenses for each property in the appropriate column.
findings.fix: Use you or your spouse in the gate, or ask whether the rental property (whoever owns it on the joint return) had any supplies.

findings.who: A filer whose property manager buys cleaning supplies out of collected rent and charges them against the rental; the filer answers no because they did not personally pay the supplier.
findings.why_no: The filer reads Supplies as an out-of-pocket payment by the filer, not supplies bought on the filer's behalf from rental income; the gate itself does not say paid, but the expense line is understood that way.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: You can deduct all ordinary and necessary expenses, such as taxes, interest, repairs, insurance, management fees, agents’ commissions, and depreciation.
findings.fix: Ask whether supplies were bought for the rental, including by an agent or manager from rental income; the amount is the cost borne by the rental, not only cash paid directly by the filer.

locators: p. 6, General Instructions for Lines 5 Through 21

findings.who: A filer receives oil or gas royalty income, has no rental real estate, and the producer withheld state or local taxes from the 2025 royalty payments.
findings.why_no: The gate is limited to 'this rental property'; the filer has royalty property, not a rental property, so the truthful answer is no. The gated help also speaks of taxes 'paid,' and these taxes were withheld by the producer rather than paid by the filer.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Enter on line 4 the gross amount of royalty income, even if state or local taxes were withheld from oil or gas payments you received. Include taxes withheld by the producer on line 16."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to rental or royalty property and ask for taxes paid or withheld, including producer-withheld taxes on oil/gas royalties; or add a separate line 16 question for royalty properties.

findings.who: A filer rents out a room or part of their personal residence in 2025 and pays property tax on the whole home; there is no separate tax bill for the rented portion.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'For this rental property — Taxes,' so they read it as asking about a separate rental property's tax and answer no; the property tax is on their home, and they do not perceive the rental portion as taxes on 'this rental property.'
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 6: "Renting out part of your home. If you rent out only part of your home or other property, deduct the part of your expenses that applies to the rented part."
findings.fix: Say the gate includes the rental portion of a home's property tax; ask about 'taxes on the rented part of this property (including part of a home)' or show the allocation rule before the gate.

locators: p. 6, Line 16

findings.who: A landlord with a rental property who has no electric, water, or gas utility bill for the rental but makes ordinary and necessary calls to the renter, or otherwise has only rental-related telephone charges.
findings.why_no: They read "Utilities" as electric/water/gas and answer no, not treating telephone calls as a line 17 utility.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 17: "You can deduct the cost of ordinary and necessary telephone calls related to your rental activities or royalty income..."
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to ask whether there were any line 17 utility/telephone expenses, expressly including ordinary and necessary calls to the renter, before any personal-use division.

findings.who: A filer with a rental property that has no rental utilities and separate royalty income, where the filer made ordinary telephone calls to licensees about the royalty.
findings.why_no: The only gate is under the rental property and asks "For this rental property — Utilities"; the filer truthfully has no rental utilities, so answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 17: "...telephone calls related to your rental activities or royalty income..."
findings.fix: Ask a separate line 17 question for royalty-related telephone calls, or move the gate out of the rental property and ask about rental or royalty telephone/utility expenses.

findings.who: A landlord whose tenant pays all utilities directly in place of rent, so the landlord receives no utility bills and pays no utility company.
findings.why_no: They answer no to "Utilities" because they did not pay any utilities themselves.
findings.irs_text: Gated line 17 (citing i1040se p. 7): "Utilities for it, paid in 2025 by you or by a tenant in place of rent."
findings.fix: Ask "Did anyone pay utilities for this rental, including a tenant who paid them in place of rent?"

findings.who: A joint filer whose spouse owns or manages the rental property and either paid its utilities or made the rental-related telephone calls; the filer personally did not.
findings.why_no: The gate does not say "you or your spouse"; the filer answers no based on their own facts.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 17: "...telephone calls related to your rental activities..." On a joint return, the spouse's line 17 amount is included.
findings.fix: Use "Did you or your spouse have any utilities or rental-related telephone calls for this property?"

findings.who: A filer who owned and rented the property for part of 2025, paying utilities or rental-related telephone charges before selling it, but who no longer owns a rental property when filing.
findings.why_no: They read "For this rental property" as requiring a current rental property and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 7, Line 17: "...telephone calls related to your rental activities..." for amounts paid in 2025.
findings.fix: Ask "At any time during 2025, did you or your spouse have utilities or rental-related telephone calls for a property that was rental property?"

findings.who: A filer with a mixed-use property whose utility bill covers both rental and personal use, who answers no because the utilities were not exclusively for the rental.
findings.why_no: They read "Utilities for it" as requiring 100% rental use; the gate does not show the helper that says to include the amount before any personal-use division.
findings.irs_text: Gated helper (citing i1040se p. 7, Line 17): "Utilities paid in 2025, before any division for personal use."
findings.fix: State in the gate: "Include the full utility amount before allocating personal use; the rental portion will be computed later."

locators: p. 7, Line 17

findings.who: A joint filer who does not personally manage the rental, but whose spouse actively participates in the current year; the rental has a prior-year unallowed loss, part of which arose in a year when neither spouse actively participated.
findings.why_no: The gate/helper is labeled only 'Active participation' and the filer reads it as asking about the filer's own participation. They truthfully answer no for themselves even though the spouse's participation makes the joint return active; the gate then skips the prior-year question.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 4: 'You aren’t considered to actively participate in a rental real estate activity if at any time during the tax year your interest (including your spouse's interest) in the activity was less than 10%'; i8582 p. 10: 'Don’t enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated in the activity in both the year the loss arose and the current tax year.'
findings.fix: Make the gate and helper explicitly per return, e.g. 'Did you or your spouse actively participate in the current tax year?', and ask the prior-year question with the same spouse-inclusive wording.

findings.who: A filer who did not make management decisions in the current year but did arrange repairs or other services in a significant and bona fide sense; the rental has a held-back loss, part of which came from a prior year without active participation.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for the legal conclusion 'Active participation', and the gated question’s wording focuses on 'helped make its decisions'. The filer answers no because they did not make decisions, missing that arranging services can count.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 4: 'You may be treated as actively participating if, for example, you participated in making management decisions or arranged for others to provide services (such as repairs) in a significant and bona fide sense.'
findings.fix: Ask facts rather than the conclusion, and include both management decisions and arranging services in the gate/help; or treat either as active participation before asking the prior-year question.

findings.who: A filer who actively participated in 2025 but did not actively participate in the earlier year in which the held-back loss arose; the 2024 return shows a prior-year unallowed loss for the rental.
findings.why_no: The gate/helper says only 'Active participation' without saying 'current tax year'. The filer reads it as active participation in both the year the loss arose and the current year, so answers no because they were not active when the loss arose.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10: 'Don’t enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated in the activity in both the year the loss arose and the current tax year. If you didn’t actively participate in both years, enter the prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part V.'
findings.fix: State 'in the current tax year' in the gate/helper, and let the gated question capture the prior-year fact; do not fold both years into the gate.

findings.who: A filer whose 2024 Form 8582, Part VII, column (c) shows a prior-year unallowed loss for the rental, but who does not recognize the phrase 'held back' as referring to that carryover.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'a loss from this rental [was] held back on the 2024 return'. The filer thinks no because they did not use that label and may not know Form 8582 Part VII column (c) is the carried-over unallowed loss.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10: 'Column (c). Enter the prior-year unallowed losses for each activity. You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582.'
findings.fix: Ask a checkable fact: 'Did your 2024 Form 8582, Part VII, column (c) show an unallowed loss for this rental?' and only then ask whether any part came from a non-active year.

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "Don’t enter a prior-year unallowed loss in column (c) of Part IV unless you actively participated in the activity in both the year the loss arose and the current tax year"
p. 4, Part IV

findings.who: A filer whose only carryover for the property is Worksheet 5-1 excess expenses from a year they used it as a home; they have no 2024 Form 8582 prior-year unallowed loss for that property.
findings.why_no: The computed branch tests "A loss from this rental held back on the 2024 return"; for this filer that helper is false, so the tool sets rental.prior_ws51_if_any to No and never asks the Worksheet 5-1 question.
findings.irs_text: Pub. 527 p. 28, Used as a home and rented 15 days or more: "The excess expenses that can’t be used to offset income from other sources are carried forward to the next year and treated as rental expenses for the same property."
findings.fix: Ask the Worksheet 5-1 question whenever rental.prior_any is yes (or whenever any loss or cost carryover exists), not only when a 2024 Form 8582 loss helper is true; broaden the helper to include Worksheet 5-1 costs.

findings.who: A filer who used a vacation home as a home and rented it 15 days or more in an earlier year, had excess expenses carried forward under Worksheet 5-1, and has no Form 8582 suspended loss.
findings.why_no: They read "loss ... held back" and the help's "Look for Form 8582" as asking only about a Form 8582 suspended loss; finding no Form 8582 entry, they say no even though the Worksheet 5-1 excess expense is carried forward.
findings.irs_text: Pub. 527 p. 28, Used as a home and rented 15 days or more: "The excess expenses that can’t be used to offset income from other sources are carried forward to the next year and treated as rental expenses for the same property."
findings.fix: Reword the gate to ask about "a rental loss or Worksheet 5-1 excess expense carried forward" and state that no Form 8582 is needed for Worksheet 5-1 carryovers.

findings.who: A joint-return filer whose spouse had a prior-year unallowed rental loss on a separate 2024 return, while the filer's own 2024 return has no such Form 8582 amount.
findings.why_no: The help says to look for Form 8582 in "your 2024 return" and asks whether "your rentals" had a loss; the filer may look only at their own return and answer no, despite the spouse parenthetical.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 10, Part IV: "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582."
findings.fix: Help should say to check both the filer's and spouse's 2024 returns, including separate returns, for Form 8582 Part VII column (c).

locators: p. 10, Part IV, "You find these amounts in Part VII, column (c), of your 2024 Form 8582"
p. 28, "The excess expenses that can’t be used to offset income from other sources are carried forward to the next year and treated as rental expenses for the same property"
p. 28, Used as a home and rented 15 days or more

findings.who: A filer whose rental activity rents more than one class of property, for example short daily rentals that bring in most of the income alongside one low-rent long lease. Take ten 3-day rentals earning 99% of gross rental income and one 365-day lease earning 1%.
findings.why_no: The help says to divide the days rented by the number of separate stays: 395 / 11 = 35.9 days, so the honest answer is no. The IRS rule weights each class's average by its share of gross rental income: 3 x 0.99 + 365 x 0.01 = 6.6 days. That is 7 days or less.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3, Exceptions: "If the activity involves renting more than one class of property, multiply the average period of customer use of each class by the ratio of the gross rental income from that class to the activity's total gross rental income. The activity's average period of customer use equals the sum of these class-by-class average periods weighted by gross income."
findings.fix: First ask whether the activity rents more than one kind of property, such as rooms and equipment, or units with different rental terms. If yes, compute the income-weighted average from per-class days, stays and gross rent. Do not use a single days-per-stay division.

findings.who: A vacation rental owner who listed the property all year (365 days) and had 10 bookings of about 4 nights each.
findings.why_no: "Days it was rented" can be read as the days the property was rented out or offered for rent, not the nights renters actually occupied it. Then 365 / 10 = 36.5 days, more than 30, so the filer answers no. The true average is about 4 days.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3, Exceptions: "dividing the total number of days in all rental periods by the number of rentals during the tax year"; exception 1a: "The average period of customer use is: a. 7 days or less"
findings.fix: Say: "Add up only the days renters actually had use of it. Do not count days it was listed or vacant, or days you used it yourself. Divide by the number of separate rentals."

findings.who: An owner whose property is booked repeatedly by the same renters, for example a corporate client that took 12 separate 5-day stays and a family that came back four times for a week.
findings.why_no: "Number of separate stays" can be read as the number of renters or customers. Counting each repeat client once shrinks the divisor and pushes the average above 30 days, or at least above 7.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3, Exceptions: "dividing the total number of days in all rental periods by the number of rentals during the tax year"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Count each rental period (booking) separately, even when the same renter comes back."

findings.who: An owner who switched in 2025 from short-term stays to a long lease, or the reverse, and also counts days in a lease or booking that started in 2024 or runs into 2026.
findings.why_no: The question has no tax-year limit, and the help example of "a one-year lease is one stay of 365 days" invites counting a whole lease that crosses years. That can raise the average above 30 even though the 2025 rental periods average 7 days or less.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 3, Exceptions: "by the number of rentals during the tax year"
findings.fix: Add "in 2025" to the question and state how to count rental periods that cross the start or end of the year.

locators: p. 3, Exceptions
p. 3, Exceptions, "Figure the average period of customer use for a class of property by dividing the total number of days in all rental periods by the number of rentals"
